title: Analysis of oxygen isotopes of inorganic phosphate (δ18Op) in freshwater: A detailed method description for obtaining oxygen isotopes of inorganic phosphate in environmental water samples
author: Nisbeth, Tamburini, et al.
materials: Furthermore, due to the complexity of the method it has been proven challenging to implement for new practitioners. This is a notable problem as the applicability of the δ18Op method is contingent upon an extended knowledge of the δ18Op signatures and understanding of the systematics of the various isotopic alteration processes [29,38].

Magnesium-induced co-precipitation can quantitatively remove dissolved Pi by adsorption onto Mg(OH)2 (brucite), initiated by addition of NaOH which raises the pH. Brucite can precipitate at any temperature, but temperatures should be kept low (5–10°C) in order to keep microbial activity at a minimum. Furthermore, the water samples need to be processed immediately after sampling to avoid potential microbial alterations. The procedure of the brucite precipitation step is as follows:(a) Discard some of the sampled water to ensure space for the reactants in the polyethylene container. (b) Add 3 M MgCl2 until the solution achieves a final concentration of ∼55 mM Mg2+ corresponding to the Mg2+ concentration found in seawater [16,35]; for example, this corresponds to the addition of 1 L of 3 M MgCl2 to 50 L freshwater sample. Mix well. (c) Then add 1 M NaOH equivalent to 0.5% of the sample solution volume [35] and mix again. Check with pH indicator strips that the pH becomes between 9 and 10, as alkaline conditions facilitate brucite precipitation better than acidic conditions [35]. If pH 9 in order to prevent the brucite (and co-precipitated phosphate) from dissolving into solution. (e) Then remove the supernatant. With large sample volumes, this can be done by siphoning or using e.g. a peristaltic pump (Fig. 1a). The brucite flocs left after removing the supernatant might make up several liters of sludge (Fig. 1b). (f) Check the absence of Pi in the supernatant, e.g. by using the spectrophotometric molybdate blue-method [26]. Discard the supernatant if Pi has been 100% stripped from the sample solution. If Pi is still present, add additional NaOH to the supernatant and combine all the precipitated brucite.Fig. 1(a) Removing the supernatant from the brucite flocs by siphoning, using a peristaltic pump. (b) Brucite flocs transferred to a beaker after discarding the supernatant.Fig 1

steps.title: Optional pre‑MagIC filtration
steps.instruction: If needed, filter the fresh‑water sample to remove particulates before the MagIC steps. Use a 0.45 µm GF/F filter, or a sequence of 1 µm then 0.2 µm polypropylene cartridge filters under low pressure; avoid slow filtration for ferrous waters.

steps.title: Magnesium‑induced co‑precipitation (MagIC)
steps.instruction: Quantitatively remove dissolved phosphate by precipitating it onto Mg(OH)₂ (brucite) at low temperature.

substeps.instruction: Discard a small volume of the sample to provide head‑space in a polyethylene container.
Add 3 M MgCl₂ until the final Mg²⁺ concentration is ≈55 mM (e.g., 1 L of 3 M MgCl₂ to 50 L of freshwater). Mix well.
Add 1 M NaOH equal to 0.5 % of the sample volume. Mix and verify pH 9–10 with indicator strips (pH 9 prevents brucite dissolution).
Keep the sample at 5–10 °C and process immediately after collection to limit microbial activity.
Allow brucite flocs to form, then remove the supernatant by siphoning or peristaltic pump, collecting the flocs (several liters of sludge may form).
Test the supernatant for residual PO₄³⁻ with the molybdate‑blue spectrophotometric method; if PO₄ remains, add more NaOH and repeat precipitation until Pi is fully removed.

steps.title: Centrifugation of brucite flocs
steps.instruction: Separate the brucite precipitate from the supernatant by centrifugation.

substeps.instruction: Transfer the brucite sludge to large centrifuge tubes (e.g., 250 mL).
Centrifuge at 3500 rpm for 10 min (recommended compromise).
Discard the clear supernatant.

steps.title: Brucite dissolution
steps.instruction: Dissolve the brucite pellet in acid to liberate the adsorbed phosphate.

substeps.instruction: Add 1 M HNO₃ to the centrifuge tubes until the brucite can be easily removed; use the minimum volume needed.
Combine the acid‑dissolved material from all tubes.
Adjust the solution to pH ≈ 1 with additional 1 M HNO₃ (use pH strips).

steps.title: Additional MagIC clean‑up (optional repeat)
steps.instruction: If the brucite suspension is discoloured (tan/brown) due to dissolved organic matter, repeat the MagIC cycle to purify Pi.

substeps.instruction: Raise the pH of the acid solution to 10–11 with 1 M NaOH (do NOT add MgCl₂).
Re‑centrifuge as in Step III and re‑dissolve as in Step IV, keeping the final pH at 1.
Repeat the raise‑pH, centrifuge, and dissolve cycle until the suspension is milky‑white (up to five repetitions).

steps.title: Final acid‑phase filtration
steps.instruction: Remove any remaining insoluble particles after the last MagIC dissolution.

substeps.instruction: Vacuum‑filter the pH ≈ 1 solution through a 0.7 µm GF/F filter (centrifuge first if needed).
Discard the filter (or retain for storage if the sample will be kept).

steps.title: Ammonium phospho‑molybdate precipitation
steps.instruction: Scavenge phosphate from the acidic solution by forming APM crystals.

substeps.instruction: Transfer the acid solution to an Erlenmeyer flask and place in a 50 °C water‑bath shaker or on a magnetic stirrer set to 50 °C.
If the solution is cold from refrigeration, allow it to reach near‑room temperature before adding reagents.
Add 25 mL of 35 % (w/w) ammonium nitrate solution.
Slowly add 40 mL of 10 % NH₄‑molybdate solution.
Adjust the pH to ≈ 1 with 1 M H₂SO₄ (≈ 1 mL, enough to avoid large volume change).
Shake gently and leave the mixture overnight at 50 °C to complete APM precipitation.

steps.title: APM crystal isolation and washing
steps.instruction: Collect and clean the APM precipitate before dissolution.

substeps.instruction: Vacuum‑filter the mixture onto a 0.2 µm cellulose acetate filter; filtration may take several hours and may require multiple filters.
Wash the retained APM crystals with >200 mL of 5 % ammonium nitrate solution.
Transfer the filter(s) with crystals to a 100 mL Erlenmeyer flask.

steps.title: APM dissolution
steps.instruction: Dissolve the APM crystals in ammonium‑citrate solution.

substeps.instruction: Add a minimum volume (15–50 mL) of NH₄‑citrate solution to the flask; start with 10 mL then add 5 mL aliquots while swirling.
Work under a fume hood; continue swirling until the solution becomes transparent (≈ 15–20 min).
Discard the filter.

steps.title: Magnesium ammonium phosphate precipitation
steps.instruction: Re‑precipitate phosphate as MAP under alkaline conditions.

substeps.instruction: Add 25 mL of the Mg‑reagent to the dissolved APM solution while stirring.
Add ~7 mL of 1:1 (NH₃ : NH₄⁺) ammonia solution.
Check pH; if < 8, add more 1:1 ammonia until pH reaches 8–9 (optimal for MAP).
Cover the flask with parafilm, puncture small vent holes, and leave on the stirrer overnight.

steps.title: MAP crystal isolation
steps.instruction: Collect MAP crystals for the next dissolution step.

substeps.instruction: Vacuum‑filter the MAP suspension onto a 0.2 µm cellulose nitrate filter; discard the supernatant.
Wash the crystals thoroughly with >200 mL of 1:20 (NH₃ : NH₄⁺) ammonia solution to remove chloride and other contaminants.

steps.title: MAP dissolution
steps.instruction: Release phosphate from MAP using dilute nitric acid.

substeps.instruction: Place the filter with MAP crystals into a 50 mL centrifuge tube.
Add 5–10 mL of 0.5 M HNO₃ (minimum volume) and shake to dissolve the crystals.
Leave the tube in contact with acid for at least 15–20 min to ensure complete dissolution.

steps.title: Cation removal with resin
steps.instruction: Scavenge Na⁺ and multivalent cations using a proton‑charged cation exchange resin.

substeps.instruction: Convert AG‑50WX8 resin to the H⁺ form by shaking with 1.5 × resin‑volume of 7 M HNO₃ overnight.
Discard the acid and rinse the resin repeatedly with 1 L de‑ionised water until the rinse water reaches pH > 5.
Filter the rinse water through a 0.45 µm polycarbonate filter (repeat rinses as needed).
Add 6 mL of the prepared resin slurry to the MAP‑dissolved sample, seal, and shake overnight.
Next day, filter the sample through a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter; rinse the resin on the filter with 1–2 mL de‑ionised water.
Collect the resin and re‑condition it in 1 M HNO₃ for future use.

steps.title: Chloride elimination
steps.instruction: Remove residual Cl⁻ by precipitating AgCl before Ag₃PO₄ formation.

substeps.instruction: Transfer the filtered sample solution to a small container (e.g., 50 mL centrifuge tube).
Add a few AgNO₃ crystals; the solution will turn whitish‑opaque as AgCl precipitates.
Wait ≥ 5 min, then re‑filter using the same 0.2 µm filter from the previous step.

steps.title: Silver phosphate precipitation (slow method)
steps.instruction: Precipitate Ag₃PO₄ crystals under controlled pH and Ag⁺ excess.

substeps.instruction: Add Ag‑ammine solution to achieve an Ag⁺ : Pi ratio of ≈ 10 : 1; the mixture will turn briefly white (pH ≈ 7) then become transparent (pH > 7).
Place the container in an oven at 50 °C. Yellow Ag₃PO₄ crystals begin to appear after a few hours; allow up to 2 days for complete precipitation.
If after 1–2 days no crystals are visible, check pH and adjust to 7 ± 0.5 using HNO₃ or NH₄OH (do NOT use HCl or NaOH).
Vacuum‑filter the crystals onto a 0.2 µm polycarbonate filter (other filter types trap crystals).
Wash the collected crystals thoroughly with de‑ionised water to remove nitrate residues.
Dry the filter with crystals at 50 °C for at least 1 day.
Optionally, perform a final wash with a few drops of H₂O₂ to oxidise residual organic matter.
Store the dried crystals in a desiccator until analysis.

steps.title: Prepare Ag₃PO₄ for IRMS
steps.instruction: Package the dried Ag₃PO₄ crystals for isotope‑ratio mass‑spectrometry.

substeps.instruction: Using a steel spatula, transfer crystals into silver thimble capsules; weigh ≈ 300 µg per capsule in triplicate.
Add a few grains of black carbon (no weighing required) to each capsule.
Close the capsules with tweezers, avoiding finger contact.
Place the sealed capsules in a 96‑well micro‑plate, cover the plate with parafilm, add the lid, and tape it shut.
